children.translated_text: Having bowed to the universal, omniscient one with the actions of mind, speech, and body,
this work called the <s>Kāvyālaṃkāra</s> will be composed according to my understanding.
Skill in <s>dharma</s>, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, and also in the arts,
as well as delight and fame, are produced by the composition of good poetry.
Just as generosity in a poor man, skill with weapons in an impotent man,
or boldness in an ignorant man, so is knowledge of śāstra in a non-poet.

children.text: vinayena vinā kā śrīḥ kā niśā śaśinā vinā
children.translated_text: Without discipline, what is beauty? Without the moon, what is night?
And without true poetic power, what sort of cleverness in speech can there be?
Even dull-minded people are able to study śāstra from a teacher’s instruction;

children.text: kāvyaṃ tu jāyate jātu kasyacit pratibhāvataḥ ||
children.translated_text: but poetry is born only rarely in someone, from native genius.
Even when the makers of compositions have reached heaven,

children.text: āsta eva nirātaṅkaṃ kāntaṃ kāvyamayaṃ vapuḥ ||
children.translated_text: their lovely body made of poetry remains here, free from harm.

children.text: ruṇaddhi rodasī cāsya yāvat kīrtir anaśvarī
children.translated_text: And as long as his imperishable fame obstructs the two worlds,

children.text: tāvat kilāyam adhyāste sukṛtī vaibudhaṃ padam ||
children.translated_text: so long, they say, this meritorious man dwells in the state of the gods.

children.text: ato 'bhivāñchatā kīrtiṃ stheyasīm ā bhuvaḥ sthiteḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore one who desires fame enduring as long as the earth stands
should, knowing what is to be known, make effort toward the characteristics of poetry.
Words, meter, denoted meanings, stories resting on history,
ordinary usage, reasoning, and the arts should be regarded as under the poet’s control.
Having understood word and meaning, having attended upon those who know them,
and having examined other compositions, one should undertake the practice of making poetry.
In every way, not even a single word should be uttered as something blameworthy;
for poetry marked by a defect is censured like a bad son.
Lack of poetic talent leads to demerit, disease, or punishment;
but bad poetry, the wise say, is death itself.
Ornaments such as simile and metaphor have been described in many ways by others;
even a lovely woman’s face does not shine when without adornment.
Others call ornaments such as metaphor external,

children.text: supāṃ tiṅāṃ ca vyutpattiṃ vācāṃ vāñchantyalaṃkṛtim ||
children.translated_text: and desire grammatical correctness of nominal and verbal endings as the ornament of speech.
They call this correctness of expression; but such is not skill in meaning.
For us, however, both kinds are desired, divided as ornaments of word and of meaning.

children.text: śabdārthau sahitau kāvyaṃ gadyaṃ padyaṃ ca taddvidhā
children.translated_text: Poetry is word and meaning joined together; it is of two kinds, prose and verse.
It is threefold as Sanskrit, Prakrit, and another form, Apabhraṃśa.
It may proclaim the deeds of gods and other figures of past tradition, or have an invented subject,
or be based on the arts and sciences; again it is divided fourfold.
The canto-composition, what is meant for performance, and likewise the ākhyāyikā and the kathā,
and unbound poetry and the like: that again is said to be fivefold.

children.text: sargabandho mahākāvyaṃ mahatāṃ ca mahacca yat
children.translated_text: A canto-composition is a mahākāvya, one that belongs to great persons and is itself great,
with no vulgar words, meaningful, furnished with ornaments, and having a worthy basis.
It includes counsel, envoys, journeys, battles, and the hero’s rise to success,
is furnished with the five junctures, is not overly explanatory, and is rich in prosperity.
Even though it expresses the four aims of life, it chiefly gives instruction in practical benefit,
and is joined with the nature of the world and with all the rasas separately.
After first presenting the hero through lineage, valor, learning, and the like,
one should not tell of that very hero’s death in order to describe another’s excellence.
If he is not intended to pervade the body of the poem,
then the initial mention and praise of one who shares in no rise to success are pointless.
Drama, dvipadī, śamyā, rāsaka, skandhaka, and the like
are said to be intended for performance; their details have been stated by others.
The ākhyāyikā is considered to be in prose, with natural, unconfused, pleasing words, meanings, compounds, and style,
and joined with a noble subject, divided into ucchvāsas.
In it the hero narrates his own conduct as what has occurred,

children.text: vaktraṃ cāparavaktraṃ ca kāle bhāvyārthaśaṃsi ca ||
children.translated_text: and it has vaktra and aparavaktra meters that at the proper time indicate future events.
It is marked by certain narrative episodes created according to the poet’s intention,
and is furnished with abduction of a maiden, battle, separation, and prosperity.
The kathā is not furnished with vaktra and aparavaktra meters, nor does it have ucchvāsas;
it may be in Sanskrit, and its action may be refined; likewise it may partake of Apabhraṃśa.

children.text: anyaiḥ svacaritaṃ tasyāṃ nāyakena tu nocyate
children.translated_text: In it the hero’s own story is told by others, not by the hero himself;
for how could a well-born person make a display of his own virtues?
Unbound poetry, again, is such things as a single gāthā or a single śloka;
all this is accepted when joined with crooked expression and natural expression.
Some other intelligent people think there is a different style called Vaidarbha,

children.text: tadeva ca kila jyāyaḥ sadarthamapi nāparam ||
children.translated_text: and that it alone is superior, while the other, though having good meaning, is not.
“This is Gauḍīya and that is Vaidarbha”: why make such a distinction?
Because of mere blind following of predecessors, various names are applied by the unintelligent.
But, it may be objected, the Aśmaka lineage and the like are called Vaidarbha.
Let it be so if you wish; generally a name is assigned according to preference.
This style, with meaning not fully developed, lacking oblique expression, clear, straight, and soft,
is distinct like something sung; it is merely pleasant to the ear.
Even the Gauḍīya style, if ornamented, non-vulgar, meaningful, reasonable, and unconfused,
is better; otherwise the Vaidarbha style is not so.
The charm of speech does not arise merely from excessive sweetness and the like;
an oblique statement of word and meaning is accepted as the ornament of speech.
Poets do not use a meaning that must be inferred, a labored one, one with another unintended sense, one that fails to denote, one without reasoning,
nor expression through obscure words.
A “meaning to be led out” is one whose meaning is forcibly drawn out by learned people through some intention of their own,
though it has not mounted upon the proper rule of words.

children.text: māyeva bhadreti yathā sā cāsādhvī prakalpanā
children.translated_text: For example, “māyā iva bhadrā”; that is an improper construction.
and, in the statement 'from bamboo and so on,' they are restricted by the wording, without anything further.
One should know the obscure to be what is separated, as when another meaning is lost, for example:

children.text: vijahrustasya tāḥ śokaṃ krīḍāyāṃ vikṛtaṃ ca tat ||
children.translated_text: 'They sported away his sorrow in play'; that expression is distorted in that way.
'The sky is filled with the enemies of the remover of snow' is non-expressive.
When the intended meaning is not directly established, the designation is not understood.
Illogical expression is such as making clouds, winds, and moons messengers,
and likewise bees, hārīta birds, cakravākas, parrots, and the like.
Some are speechless, some have manifest speech, and some move in distant regions;

children.text: kathaṃ dūtyaṃ prapadyeranniti yuktyā na yujyate ||
children.translated_text: how could they undertake the work of messengership? Thus it does not accord with reason.
But if, through longing, he speaks this or that like a madman,
then let it be so; in abundance this is employed by the intelligent.
The use of words with hidden denotation is never to be employed in any way;
even for the wise this is not fit to render assistance.
'Asitartitugadricchit, lord of heaven and earth, seer of the mountainless,'
'with these bright-eyed seers may he wish to strike down your enemies.'
Faulty in sound and faulty in meaning, and also what is called faulty through supposition,
and likewise harsh to hear: they call these the fourfold fault of speech.
Words such as feces, excrement, settled filth, wetness, cutness, vomit, flowing,
course, violation, belching, discharge, the sound 'ha,' and constriction,
'golden-seeded,' 'narrow passage,' 'soft,' 'approached by egg-born beings,'
and 'speech-thorn' and the like are considered utterances faulty to the ear.
Faulty in meaning, again, should be known where, after it is uttered, an idea arises
whose object is an indecorous thing, through words that denote it, as for example:
For one who has set out only to kill, who is rigid and seeks openings,
a fall certainly occurs; rising again comes only with difficulty.
When something undesirable is imagined in the junction of two words,
they call that faulty through supposition, as in 'possessing heroism as ornament.'
And expressions such as 'yathā jihladadityādi' they know to be harsh to hear;
skilled poets do not desire that; others, indeed, do not even desire 'gaṇḍa.'
Yet because of a special arrangement, even what is badly said shines,
like a blue palāśa flower bound in the midst of garlands.
Something improper too acquires beauty from the beauty of its support,
like dark collyrium placed on a beloved woman's eyes.
'This face, O lotus-eyed woman, has pale cheeks';
because of the conjunction with the word 'pale,' the word 'cheek' is proper, as stated.
By this rule one should understand other cases too, where even an improper word is fitting,
as in 'of elephants whose cheeks are wet with ichor-water.'
'Four hundred elephants with cheeks wet from rutting ichor,'
just as that is so, so too one may employ both the less proper and the more proper.

children.text: etad grāhyaṃ surabhi kusumaṃ grāmyametannidheyaṃ dhatte śobhāṃ viracitamidaṃ sthānamasyaitadasya
children.translated_text: 'This fragrant flower is to be taken; this rustic one is to be set aside; this arranged one bears beauty; this is its proper place,'

children.text: mālākāro racayati yathā sādhu vijñāya mālāṃ yojyaṃ kāvyeṣvavahitadhiyā tadvad evābhidhānam ||
children.translated_text: just as a garland-maker, knowing well, makes a garland, so in poems expression must be joined by one whose mind is attentive.
The intelligent, desiring sweetness and clarity,
do not employ words that are for the most part full of compounds.
Some, wishing to express forcefulness, compound many words together,
as in 'she whose locks are tawny with the pollen of mandāra flowers.'
Poetry is considered sweet when its meaning is audible and not overly compounded,
and clear when its meaning is understood even by learned women and children.
Alliteration, together with yamaka, metaphor, dīpaka, and simile:
these five alone are cited by others as ornaments of speech.
They declare <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) to be an arrangement of similar phonemes,
as in the stated example, 'What is the use of that thought, beloved, so excessive?'
But another kind they, the wise, regard as rustic alliteration:
'Mighty <s>Bala</s>, his throat filled with a swarm of restless blue bees among swinging garlands.'
Alliterations should have varied meanings and should not have dissimilar syllables;
by this moderate rule charming utterances are produced.
Some here also accept the Lāṭīya type of alliteration, as for example:
'Cast a gaze pleasing to the eyes; the moon has risen from the moon-faced one.'
Initial, medial, and final yamaka, repetition of a pāda, and a row,
and yamaka of the whole pāda: this is said to be fivefold.
Forms such as <s>saṃdaṣṭaka</s> and <s>samudga</s> are considered included within this very classification;
it may occur at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end; therefore it is just fivefold, as follows:

children.text: sādhunā sādhunā tena rājatā rājatā bhṛtā
children.translated_text: 'By that good man, good, bearing shining silverness, shining,'

children.text: sahitaṃ sahitaṃ kartuṃ saṃgataṃ saṃgataṃ janam ||
children.translated_text: 'fitly joined, joined, to make the assembled, assembled, people.'

children.text: sādhuḥ saṃsārādbibhyadasmādasārāt kṛtvā kleśāntaṃ yāti vartma praśāntam
children.translated_text: 'A good man, fearing this worthless saṃsāra, having made an end of affliction, goes on the tranquil path;'

children.text: jātiṃ vyādhīnāṃ durnayānāmadhīnāṃ vāñchan tyāyastvaṃ chinddhi muktānayastvam ||
children.translated_text: 'cut off birth, subjection to diseases and bad policies, your painful longing; be one whose way is liberation.'

children.text: na te dhīr dhīra bhogeṣu ramaṇīyeṣu saṃgatā
children.translated_text: Your mind, O steadfast one, is not attached to delightful pleasures;
these women, when connected with them, carry away even sages.
Her eyes are white and black, her breasts and lips are lovely, she is full of joy, clearly intoxicated, with a splendid mark of intoxication;

children.text: ghanā ghanā nīlaghanāghanālakāṃ priyāmimāmutsukayanti yanti ca ||
children.translated_text: dense, dense, dark-cloud-like are her heavy dark-cloud tresses; they excite this beloved woman, and they go.
These kings, who have issued complete commands, whose authority is never obstructed at any time,
are punishers of offenders and road-breakers, seated on such thrones inherited in paternal succession.
In this way, in immediately adjacent and separated pādas, and also at the ends of pādas,

children.text: kṛtsnaṃ ca sarvapādeṣu duṣkṛtaṃ sādhu tādṛśam ||
children.translated_text: and in all pādas as a whole, such difficult composition is proper.
Of expressions alike in sound but mutually different in their denoted meanings...
The repetition of syllables is called <s>yamaka</s>.
Recognizable in wording, forceful, and having well-joined compounds,

children.text: prasādi svabhidhānaṃ ca yamakaṃ kṛtināṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: clear and self-expressive: such <s>yamaka</s> is approved by skilled poets.
A riddle that is deep with various verbal roots and meanings,
and that goes by the name <s>yamaka</s>, has been stated in the answer to <s>Rāmaśarman</s> and <s>Acyuta</s>.
But if these poems too are to be understood only through explanation, like technical treatises,

children.text: utsavaḥ sudhiyāmeva hanta durmedhaso hatāḥ vā ||
children.translated_text: then, alas, they are a festival only for the wise, while people of poor understanding are lost.
When the real nature of the object compared is represented through the standard of comparison,

children.text: guṇānāṃ samatāṃ dṛṣṭvā rūpakaṃ nāma tadviduḥ ||
children.translated_text: because equality of qualities is seen, that is known as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor).
It may have the whole object as its domain, or may turn on only one part.
Thus <s>rūpaka</s> is said to be twofold; this same point is now stated with examples.
The lofty cloud-elephants, streaming spray-water as rut-fluid,
emerge and adorn this forest of <s>Śakra</s>'s bows.
Of the rain-clouds girdled with circles of lightning and bearing garlands of cranes,

children.text: payomucāṃ dhvanirdhīro dunoti mama tāṃ priyām ||
children.translated_text: the deep sound torments that beloved of mine.
<s>Dīpaka</s> is held to be threefold, according as it concerns the beginning, middle, or end,
because one and the same thing has three positions; therefore it is divided in three ways.
These examples make its name meaningful, since they illuminate the sense.
This threefold type is indicated by three illustrations as follows.
Intoxication produces delight, together with love, fragile with wounded pride;
it produces longing for union with the beloved, and an unbearable grief of the mind.
Spring adorns women wearing garlands and fine garments,
and also the slopes of mountains with the cries of green parrots.
The hot season seeks to bring to an end forests full of cicadas, rivers with drying water,
and the minds of travelers abroad.
When, by a standard of comparison opposed in place, time, action, and the like,
similarity to the object compared is established through a slight trace of quality, that is <s>upamā</s> (simile).
The words <s>yathā</s> and <s>iva</s> express resemblance between two distinct things:
for example, 'dark like a blade of <s>dūrvā</s> grass,' and 'a slender woman like a dark creeper.'
Another kind, without the words <s>yathā</s> and <s>iva</s>, is expressed by a compound:
for example, 'lotus-petal-eyed' and 'moon-faced.'
With the suffix <s>vat</s> too, similarity of action is expressed in just the same way:
'He studies like a twice-born man, and instructs us like a teacher.'
By placing the same thing in a parallel counterpart, <s>prativastūpamā</s> is expressed,
even without the statement of <s>yathā</s> or <s>iva</s>, because similarity of quality is understood.
Here a quality such as being common to good and ordinary things is distinguished;
that quality brings about likeness, even when there is opposition between the two, as in the following.
How many possess qualities marked by a beauty common to the noble and the ordinary?
And how many roadside trees bend low with fruits sweet when ripe?
Some great authorities have stated that this simile is of three kinds;
that is explained here as due to the divisions of blame, praise, and the desire to describe.
Surely all three are already stated through the mention of a general quality.
All the elaboration beginning with garland-simile is not superior; it is needless expansion.
Inferiority, impossibility, difference of gender and number, reversal,
excess of the standard of comparison, and also dissimilarity on that account:
these seven faults of simile have been stated by intelligent men.
Here they are described separately, with examples and defining marks.
He, with yellow garment shaken by the wind, gracefully bearing a moon-bright lotus,
the foremost of the <s>Yadus</s>, holding the <s>Śārṅga</s> bow, appeared like a cloud with <s>Indra</s>'s rainbow.
Here, by mentioning <s>Śakra</s>'s bow, the bow is indeed shown;
but since the garment and conch are not taken up, it is called deficient.

children.text: sarvaṃ sarveṇa sārūpyaṃ nāsti bhāvasya kasyacit
children.translated_text: There is no complete resemblance of anything with anything in every respect.
Skilled poets use similes according to what is appropriate.
Where is the moon with its unbroken disk, and where the radiant face of a beloved woman?
It is compared with the moon only because of some general quality of brightness.
Some poems of great poets must be interpreted by implication.
Or has total resemblance been seen, as stated in <s>Rājamitra</s>?
When their eyes were closed by the sun's rays, when they were wretched and their lotus-breeze pride was gone,

children.text: sādhvyaḥ svageheṣviva bhartṛhīnāḥ kekā vineśuḥ śikhināṃ mukheṣu ||
children.translated_text: the cries of the peacocks disappeared in their mouths like virtuous wives in their own homes without their husbands.
Bright arrows came forth from his mouth, as it were, occupying the middle of the bow's circle,
like blazing streams of water from the haloed sun at midday.
How can there be a fall of blazing water-streams from the sun?
Because this is impossible by reason, it is therefore called impossibility.
What skilled poet would make a simile with an impossible object?
Who indeed would compare the moon, marked with the hare, to fire?
How can an object possessing excess be regarded as impossible?
And excess of meaning is accepted in simile and poetic imagining, as in the following.
This elephant appears like darkness massed together.
A lake with clear autumn water appears like a piece of sky cast down.
Now difference of gender and number are stated, together with their reversals.
Because of inferiority and superiority, that fault is twofold; all three are illustrated as follows.
You are unfathomable even to women whose minds are fixed on no one else,
like a river whose waves are split by rough stones to one wishing to cross it.
Advancing in front at one place, rushing upon and striking at another,

children.text: śuneva sāraṅgakulaṃ tvayā bhinnaṃ dviṣāṃ balam ||
children.translated_text: you broke the army of enemies, a herd of antelopes, like a dog.
This <s>cakravāka</s> bird, seated on a lotus-seat, shines forth
like the blessed <s>Brahmā</s> at the beginning of an age, wishing to create beings.
But, one may object, the hand is compared with a blossoming lotus.
The lower lip is spoken of in connection with the gleam of a piece of coral and with the bimba fruit.
One may say that this is indeed possible, but this rule concerning woman and man
is not approved by others, nor is it accepted for all three cases.

children.text: sa pītavāsāḥ pragṛhītaśārṅgo manojñabhīmaṃ vapurāpa kṛṣṇaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, wearing yellow garments and holding the <s>Śārṅga</s> bow, assumed a form charming and terrible,
like a cloud at night joined with the moon and bearing lightning as <s>Indra</s>'s bow.

children.text: śaśino grahaṇād etadādhikyaṃ kila na hy ayam
children.translated_text: Because the moon is eclipsed, there is indeed an excess here; for this cloud

children.text: nirdiṣṭa upameye'rthe vācyo vā jalado'tra tu ||
children.translated_text: is not stated in the object compared, nor should it be explicitly expressed here.
Thus the rule has been stated at length: there is not likeness in every respect.
Because of the poet's intention, one should not here understand a lotus.
A superiority of the standards of comparison is proper; there should not be excessive superiority:
fame is like cow's milk, jasmine, and <s>Halin</s> in purity.
Surely likeness is expressed by one object of comparison alone.

children.text: uktārthasya prayogo hi gurumarthaṃ na puṣyati ||
children.translated_text: For the use of an already stated meaning does not nourish a weighty meaning.
Then, in that forest, rutting elephants with temples moist from streaming ichor, following the females,
and peacocks adorned with variegated tail-feathers, shone like stainless-bodied planets in heaven.
If likeness of elephants and the like is expressed even with planets,

children.text: tathāpi teṣāṃ tair asti kāntir vāpyugratāpi vā ||
children.translated_text: even so, they have either beauty or fierceness in common with those.
Thus a variety of <s>upamā</s> (simile) has been stated; another will again be described.
A further distinction apart from ornaments beginning with <s>upamā</s> is set forth.
<s>Ākṣepa</s> (implied objection), <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (statement of another supporting sense), <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast), <s>vibhāvanā</s> (imaginative causeless effect),
<s>samāsokti</s> (compressed expression), and <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbolic statement) are six further ornaments.
Among these, <s>ākṣepa</s>, whose object is something to be stated or already stated, is considered twofold;
the remaining ones, each in a single form, will be described in order.
What is like a denial of what is desired, with the intention of expressing a special point,

children.text: ākṣepa iti taṃ santaḥ śaṃsanti dvividhaṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: the learned call that <s>ākṣepa</s>; it is twofold, as follows.

children.text: ahaṃ tvāṃ yadi nekṣeya kṣaṇamapyutsukā tataḥ
children.translated_text: 'If, longing for you, I should not see you even for a moment,
let just this much be; what need is there for any other unpleasant speech?'
'It is strange that you have no arrogance, though the limit of your valor is the earth.
What bank could be sufficient to disturb the ocean?'
The presentation of another meaning apart from the one stated
is to be known as <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s>, following the previous meaning, as in:
'You have no fear, though you wish to enter dreadful enemy armies.

children.text: sādhu vāsādhu vāgāmi puṃsām ātmaiva śaṃsati ||
children.translated_text: Whether good or bad is coming, a man's own self announces it.'
By the word 'hi' too, because it reveals the sense of cause for establishing what has been said,
this <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> is expressed still more clearly, as in:
'Mountains bear clouds that have come to them, though they are heavy;
for only one who is weightier bears the heavy ones who have come through affection.'
The showing of a special quality in an object that has a standard of comparison
is considered <s>vyatireka</s>, because it assigns a distinction, as in:
'Your eyes are white and black, furnished with lashes, and marked with reddish streaks;
but the white lotus and the blue lotus are entirely white and dark.'
When an action is denied, the imagining of its result
is to be known precisely as <s>vibhāvanā</s>, provided that a natural explanation is easy.
'The peacocks are intoxicated without having drunk; the quarters are restless though not longing;
the kadamba is fragrant though not anointed, and the water is pure though its impurity has not fallen away.'
Where, when one thing is stated, another meaning is understood, having the same qualifiers,
that is called <s>samāsokti</s>, because its meaning is compressed, as in:
'This tree has a trunk, is straight, free from snakes, firm, and has many great fruits;
it has grown tall, and yet it has been thrown down by the wind.'
Speech that, because of a cause, has a range beyond ordinary worldly experience
they regard as <s>atiśayokti</s>, as an ornament, as in:
'Concealed by the moonlight that moved with the splendor of their own blossoms,
the saptacchada trees were inferred from the sound of rows of bees.'
'If water were to have a skin shed like that of snakes,
then white garments would appear on the limbs of women in the water.'
Beginning with such cases, all <s>atiśayokti</s> has been stated as joined with an excess of qualities;
one should reason it out in every case according to the tradition.
All this is indeed <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression); through it the meaning is made manifest.
A poet must make effort in this; what ornament is there without it?
<s>Hetu</s> (cause), <s>sūkṣma</s> (subtlety), and <s>leśa</s> (slight indication) are not regarded as ornaments,
because they name an aggregate and do not express <s>vakrokti</s>.
'The sun has set; the moon shines; the birds go to their resting place'—
what poetry is there in such statements? They call this mere report.
Next, the wise know two ornaments, <s>yathāsaṃkhya</s> (correspondence in order) and <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic supposition);
<s>utprekṣā</s> is sometimes called <s>saṃkhyāna</s>.
A subsequent reference, in order, to many previously stated things that have different properties
is called <s>yathāsaṃkhya</s>.
Lotus, moon, bees, elephants, male cuckoos, and peacocks
have been conquered by you with your face, beauty, eyes, gait, voice, and hair.
When the common property is not intended, and there is some connection with a simile,
through conjunction with a quality or action that is not actually its own, it is <s>utprekṣā</s>, endowed with excess.
Under the designation of a kiṃśuka tree, having climbed the tree on every side,
fire seems to look at the forest to see what is burned and what is unburned.
Some declare <s>svabhāvokti</s> (description of natural behavior) to be an ornament.
The nature of a thing is said to be its being in just that state, as in:
Shouting, calling others, running forward, and driving them in circles,
a boy keeps the cows away from the field of grain with a stick.
This has been stated in summary; expansion would only weary the intellect.
Other material too, though not collected here, should be inferred according to this method.

children.text: svayaṃ kṛtair eva nidarśanairiyaṃ mayā prakﾱptā khalu vāgalaṃkṛtiḥ
children.translated_text: This ornamentation of speech has indeed been arranged by me with examples composed by myself.
After this, another method of ornamenting speech, charming because it is manifold, will be set forth.
<s>Preyas</s> (the beloved), <s>rasavat</s> (possessing rasa), <s>ūrjasvin</s> (vigorous), <s>paryāyokta</s> (indirectly expressed), and <s>samāhita</s> (well-composed),
and <s>udātta</s> (elevated), of two kinds, and <s>śliṣṭa</s> (ambiguous), with its three divisions;
<s>apahnuti</s> (denial), <s>viśeṣokti</s> (particular statement), <s>viśeṣa</s> (distinction), and <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal connection),
and <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of what is not the topic), <s>vyājastuti</s> (praise by pretext), and <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration);
<s>upamārūpaka</s> (simile-metaphor), and also another, <s>upameyopamā</s> (reciprocal simile),
as well as <s>sahokti</s> (joint statement) and <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange), together with <s>sasaṃdeha</s> (with doubt) and <s>ananvaya</s> (without parallel);
and some call another figure <s>utprekṣāvayava</s> (a member of poetic imagining), and others call another <s>saṃsṛṣṭa</s> (combined),
and the wise have declared <s>bhāvikatva</s> (vivid presentation) also to be an ornament.
<s>Preyas</s> is as when <s>Vidura</s> said to <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, who had come to his house:

children.text: adya yā mama govinda jātā tvayi gṛhāgate
children.translated_text: 'The joy, <s>Govinda</s>, that has arisen in me today because you have come to my house
would, in time, arise only again through your own coming.'
<s>Rasavat</s> is that in which a rasa such as erotic sentiment is clearly displayed, as in:
'The queen, no ascetic woman with <s>dharma</s> concealed, came to the meeting.'
<s>Ūrjasvin</s> is as when, after <s>Karṇa</s> had returned to <s>Pārtha</s>,
'Does <s>Karṇa</s> fit the arrow twice, O <s>Śalya</s>?' Thus the snake was rejected.
<s>Paryāyokta</s> is when something is expressed in another manner;
for example, the bearer of the <s>Śārṅga</s> bow spoke to the <s>Caidya</s> at the stealing of the jewel:
'We who study do not eat food in houses or on roads;
and twice-born men do not eat that, in order to avoid the giving of its flavor.'
<s>Samāhita</s> is as, in the <s>Rājamitra</s>, <s>Nārada</s> was seen in front
of the kṣatriya women who were going because of their attachment to <s>Rāma</s>.
<s>Rāma</s>, powerful and exalted, obeying the words of his elders,
abandoned the kingdom that had come to him and went to the forest.
Others know this very same figure otherwise, under another explanation:
that which is furnished with many jewels and the like is indeed called <s>udātta</s>.
For example, when <s>Cāṇakya</s> came at night to <s>Nanda</s>'s pleasure-house,
he entered it, covered with moonstones, through masses of water.
When the true nature of the subject of comparison is established by the standard of comparison,
through quality, action, or name, that is called <s>śliṣṭa</s> (ambiguous).
This same definition is observed in metaphor too; but here
the simultaneous use of the standard of comparison and the subject compared is intended.
'The lofty cloud-elephants, letting loose sprays of water as rut-fluid,'
here the clouds and elephants are referred to at the same time.
Because of ambiguity in both meaning and word, a division of this figure is made:
successively from the mention of joint statement, simile, and cause, as follows.
Possessing shade, free from serpents, easy to ascend, and fruit-bearing,
the great roadside trees exist only for the benefit of others.
Lofty, loved by the people, great, and pouring abundant rain,
good kings, like clouds, calm the heat of the earth.
Because it has jewels, because it is unfathomable, because it does not overstep its own boundary,
and because it is the abode of many beings, there is similarity with the ocean.
<s>Apahnuti</s> is desired when there is a certain implicit simile;
its expression is made through denial of the actual fact, as in:

children.text: neyaṃ virauti bhṛṅgālī madena mukharā muhuḥ
children.translated_text: 'This is not a swarm of bees, noisy again and again with intoxication;
this is the sound of <s>Kandarpa</s>'s bow as it is being drawn.'
When one part has disappeared and another quality remains established,
that is considered <s>viśeṣokti</s>, for the purpose of making a special feature manifest, as in:

children.text: sa ekas trīṇi jayati jaganti kusumāyudhaḥ
children.translated_text: He alone, the flower-armed god, conquers the three worlds,

children.text: haratāpi tanuṃ yasya śambhunā na hṛtaṃ balam ||
children.translated_text: whose body was taken by <s>Śambhu</s>, yet whose power was not taken.
The statement of another action opposed to a quality or an action,
for the sake of expressing a special feature, is known by the wise as <s>virodha</s> (contradiction).
Though this road is cool from the shade of groves grown near it,
it burns your enemies, even those in distant lands.
When equality of quality with something superior is intended for what is inferior too,
because of connection with the same action, that is called <s>tulyayogitā</s>.

children.text: śeṣo himagiristvaṃ ca mahānto guravaḥ sthirāḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Śeṣa</s>, <s>Himagiri</s>, and you are great, weighty, and firm,
since, without overstepping your bounds, you bear the moving earth.
Praise of some other thing which is removed from the present subject
is <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>; it is explained in this way, as in:
Sweet, pleasing to those who love it, ripened at the proper time, and abundant,
behold the fruit of trees, produced without human effort.
When someone who wishes to establish a certain equality does so

children.text: kiṃcid vidhitsoryā nindā vyājastutir asau yathā ||
children.translated_text: through censure under the guise of praising qualities that are far superior, that is <s>vyājastuti</s>, as in:

children.text: rāmaḥ saptābhinat sālān giriṃ krauñcaṃ bhṛgūttamaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Rāma</s> pierced seven <s>sāla</s> trees, and the best of the <s>Bhṛgus</s> pierced <s>Krauñca</s> mountain;

children.text: śatāṃśenāpi bhavatā kiṃ tayoḥ sadṛśaṃ kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: what have you done that is like even a hundredth part of those two deeds?
Because the intended object is shown simply through a distinctive action,
one should know the figure called <s>nidarśanā</s>, without words such as <s>yathā</s> and <s>iva</s>.
This sun, with dimmed brilliance, is about to go toward setting,
instructing people that rise is for the sake of fall.
When it establishes the state of the subject compared by means of the standard of comparison,
while calling it a simile, this is <s>upamārūpaka</s>, as in:
Victorious is the foot of the discus-bearer, a measuring rod of the whole expanse of the sky,
a fresh mirror for the moon-face of perfected fortune.
Where the status of standard of comparison and subject compared exists in alternation,
that is called <s>upameyopamā</s>, as it has been stated, as in:
Fragrant, pleasing to the eye, and reddened by the intoxication of wine,
your face is like a lotus; the lotus is like your face.
Where two actions, occurring at the same time and resting on two objects,

children.text: padenaikena kathyete sahoktiḥ sā matā yathā ||
children.translated_text: are expressed by a single word, that is regarded as <s>sahokti</s> (joint statement), as in the following.
The quarters are clouded by snowfall and are causes for close embraces;
the nights grow longer together with the pleasures of lovers.
When a particular object is taken up through the exclusion of another,
that is <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange), possessing the nature of another-meaning statement, as in the following.
Having given wealth to petitioners, he acquired the wealth of fame;
this is the unfailing vow of good men who belong to all the world.

children.text: upamānena tattvaṃ ca bhedaṃ ca vadataḥ punaḥ
children.translated_text: Again, when a statement, while speaking of identity and difference by means of a standard of comparison,
serves for praise, they know that doubtful statement as <s>sasaṃdeha</s> (with doubt), as in the following.

children.text: kimayaṃ śaśī na sa divā virājate kusumāyudho na dhanurasya kausumam
children.translated_text: Is this the moon? No, it does not shine by day. Is it the flower-weaponed god? No, his bow is not made of flowers.

children.text: iti vismayādvimṛśato'pi me matistvayi vīkṣate na labhate'rthaniścayam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, though I ponder in wonder, my mind, looking at you, does not reach certainty about the object.
Where, by that very thing, there is the relation of standard and subject of comparison for that same thing,
because dissimilarity is intended, they call that <s>ananvaya</s> (non-connection).
Your face, encircled by the redness of betel and flashing with the radiance of teeth,
with eyes like blue lotuses, is like your own face.
When something connected through a compact expression of meaning is joined with a little poetic imagining,
and again with the meaning of metaphor, it is an element of <s>utprekṣā</s>, as in the following.
Because its rise and setting are alike, when the shining sun has gone to its setting,
the day, wearied, seems to enter the house of darkness for lodging.
<s>Saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination), a fine adornment, is formed by the union of many ornaments,
like a garland of jewels; and it too is stated in this way, as follows.
Between you two, both having depth and lightness and abundant treasures,
you are easy for people to resort to, while the ocean is hard to grasp.
Your face, lovely and unadorned, has the brilliance of a lotus.
For one naturally beautiful, made by the night-maker, what adornment can there be?
Combinations in other cases too should be made in this manner.
How much can I say to those whose understanding has only been stirred open?
They call <s>bhāvikatva</s> a quality belonging to a composition,
where past and future things are seen as if directly before the eyes.
Vividness, nobility, and marvelousness of meaning in the story, its being well enacted by itself,
and absence of confusion in the words: these they declare to be its causes.
Some also regard benediction as an ornament.
Its use is when the utterance is not opposed to good-heartedness, as in the following.

children.text: asmin jahīhi suhṛdi praṇayābhyasūyām āśliṣya gāḍham amumānatamādareṇa
children.translated_text: Abandon loving jealousy toward this friend; embracing him closely and respectfully, though he is not bowed down,

children.text: vindhyaṃ mahāniva ghanaḥ samaye'bhivarṣann ānandajair nayanavāribhirukṣatu tvām ||
children.translated_text: may he sprinkle you with tears born of joy, like a great cloud raining in season upon the <s>Vindhya</s>.
May the world of kings behold the cities of your enemies, whose halls are shattered by rut-blind elephants, whose best warriors are slain, whose frightened citizens have fled,

children.text: tvattejasā dagdhasamastaśobhā dviṣāṃ puraḥ paśyatu rājalokaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and whose entire splendor has been burned away by your majesty.

children.text: girāmalaṃkāravidhiḥ savistaraḥ svayaṃ viniścitya dhiyā mayoditaḥ
children.translated_text: The rule of ornaments of speech, in full detail, has been determined by myself with my own intellect and stated.
Adorned by this, the speech of those who know word and meaning shines like a woman adorned by a skilled jeweler.
Meaningless, useless, identical in meaning, doubtful, out of sequence,
deficient in word, fallen from caesura, with broken metre, and with faulty junction,
opposed to place, time, art, world usage, logic, and scripture,
and lacking proposition, reason, or example: what is faulty is not desired.
<s>Apārtha</s> means devoid of meaning; and that meaning belongs to word and sentence.
A collection of phonemes that has meaning, ending in a nominal or verbal inflection, is a word.
A collection of words mutually dependent on one another,
free from further expectancy and tied to one object, is a sentence.
In phonemes that occur in sequence, no collection or the like is possible;
but this is possible in cognition, though the elements are different at every moment.
Others say that a sentence is an understanding whose object is the final word,
with memory implanted by the preceding phonemes, since words are momentary and perish.

children.text: atrāpi bahu vaktavyaṃ jāyate tattu noditam
children.translated_text: Here too much could be said, but it is not stated.
What need is there for dispute with teachers? The matter at hand is being explained.
That which lacks the meaning of a whole is considered <s>apārthaka</s> (meaningless),
as has been stated in examples such as 'ten pomegranates, six cakes.'
What is judged <s>vyartha</s> (useless) has an obstructed meaning, while what is contradictory is taught
as causing reversal because the earlier and later meanings conflict, as in the following.

children.text: sakhi mānaṃ priye dhehi laghutāmasya mā gamaḥ
children.translated_text: Friend, put pride in your beloved; do not fall into lowliness before him.

children.text: bhartuśchandānuvartinyaḥ prema ghnanti na hi striyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For women who follow their husband's wishes do not destroy love.
Because you have attended upon elders, you are among those whose enemies, the senses, have been conquered.
Now remain merely as a receptacle of discipline for the sake of the highest good.
What has no difference of meaning from something else is called <s>ekārtha</s> (same in meaning).
Others call this repetition, because of the distinction between word and meaning.
But repetition of the word is not described here because of its grossness.
How could one whose mind has been caught up say again just what has already been said?
In fear, grief, jealousy, joy, and wonder too,

children.text: yathāha gaccha gaccheti punaruktaṃ ca tadviduḥ ||
children.translated_text: as when one says, 'Go, go!' they know that to be repetition.
Here, repetition of meaning is what is considered <s>ekārtha</s>.
It occurs in restating what has already been said, when no purpose is possible, as in the following.
Surely the sound of waters makes her mind eager,
waters released by clouds and falling through the mouths of spouts on the palaces.
When only general properties are heard and the specific instance is not mentioned,
knowledge that does not settle on one thing is known as doubt.
Therefore the expression that produces that is called <s>sasaṃśaya</s> (doubtful).

children.text: iṣṭaṃ niścitaye vākyaṃ na velāyeti tadyathā ||
children.translated_text: A sentence that is intended for a definite conclusion should not be out of time, as in the following:
Having snakes, hard to climb, possessing jewels, and bearing fruits,
the uneven mountains quickly bring fear to the careless.
Here, when the indication follows the sequence of the instruction, it is considered sequence;
when it lacks that, through reversal, it is called <s>apakramam</s>, disorder of sequence.
Wearing diadems and moons, dark like rainclouds and bright like snow,
bearing the discus and trident, may <s>Śambhu</s> and the bearer of <s>Śārṅga</s> protect you.
What, because of the approved usage of the sūtra-maker and the commentator, would otherwise be different,
the trustworthy hearers, on the authority of established usage, know to be faulty in word, as in the following:
Look at the clouds in daytime, ringed with flashing lightning,

children.text: tejas tirayataḥ sauraṃ ghanān paśya divābhitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: vast and heavy with spread-out masses of water, obscuring the sun's radiance.
The examination of the pause in words established by meter
when lacking that is called 'fallen from the pause,' as in the following:
These rainclouds, having lightning and bodies dark as <s>tamāla</s> trees, roar.
The arrangement of a heavy or light syllable in an improper place,
or its deficiency or excess, is this 'different meter,' as in the following:
The swarm of bees wanders in the groves, this one intoxicated,
and you ought to go today, deprived of your beloved woman.
O beloved ones, when the two, <s>Śambhu</s> and <s>Śarvāṇī</s>, whose head-jewel is the moon, are raising their rays,

children.text: pātāṃ vaḥ śambhuśarvāṇyāv iti prāhur visaṃdhyadaḥ ||
children.translated_text: may they protect you: this, they say, is a fault of bad sandhi.
When the occurrence of some substance in a certain region is not taught,
that is to be understood as contradictory to that very thing by nature, as it is stated in the following:
On <s>Malaya</s>, near the mouths of caves, where black aloe trees grow,
the deodar trees shine, bending with fragrant blossoms.
Time is divided, according to the division of the six seasons, as if into six parts;
what makes contradiction to that, through reversal, they call a fault, as in the following:
These mango trees, beautiful in the forest, blossoming, perfume
the rainy-season winds that have taken on a shower of winter cold.
Art is skill in calculation, and the crafts are its sphere;
in the same way, they call what is reversed a maker of contradiction to that, as in the following:
From <s>ṛṣabha</s>, from that fifth note, <s>dhaivata</s> together with <s>ṣaḍja</s> is remembered;
for this is the <s>madhyamagrāma</s>, with <s>ṛṣabha</s> pressed by <s>madhyama</s>.
Thus, through delusion, one understands a settled matter in quite another way;
in other arts too, contradiction of what is to be expressed should be stated in this manner.
Those who know reality understand the world as divided into stationary and moving things;
and its usage here, when it contradicts that, makes such a contradiction, as in the following:
From drops of rut-fluid fallen from the temple-slopes of those elephants
there began a terrible river carrying elephants, horses, and chariots.
The foamy water fallen from the mouths of the army's running mounts
made the roads in every direction into water knee-deep.

children.text: nyāyaḥ śāstraṃ trivargoktidaṇḍanītiṃ ca tāṃ viduḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāya</s> is śāstra; they know it as the statement of the three aims of life and as the science of punishment.
Therefore what is wanted to contradict <s>nyāya</s>, being at odds with it, is as in the following:
Having introduced <s>Vatsesha</s> as wishing to conquer and as experienced through age,
afterwards he nevertheless declared that same capable man to be without spies.
That elephant disguise, filled within by a hundred warriors and led by <s>Sālaṅkāyana</s>,
though of that kind and standing on his own ground, he did not recognize.
Or if it was disregarded by his ministers for the accomplishment of their own interest,

children.text: aho nu mandimā teṣāṃ bhaktirvā nāsti bhartari ||
children.translated_text: ah, how great was their dullness, or else they had no devotion to their master.
What inference is this, that arrows released from strong bows by angry enemies
will fall while avoiding his vital points?

children.text: hato 'nena mama bhrātā mama putraḥ pitā mama
children.translated_text: 'He killed my brother; he killed my son, my father,
my maternal uncle and my sister's son,' their minds inflamed with anger,
many men, hurling various weapons in battle at the offender,
would not kill him, alone in another forest? How could that be?
Homage to those learned men who, knowing policy,
set aside both śāstra and common experience and lead this intention of the poet in just that way.
Even a child knows the difference between a living forest elephant

children.text: viśeṣaṃ veda bālo'pi kaṣṭaṃ kiṃ nu kathaṃ nu tat ||
children.translated_text: and one made of hide. What hardship is there? How indeed could that be?
Authoritative tradition, the <s>dharmaśāstras</s>, and the boundary of worldly usage are made by that;
what contradicts that, through transgression of that conduct, is as in the following:
While mountain-kings, drinkers of soma, stood on the proper path,
and while a preceptor was present, a man wishing to conquer and to adorn his lineage,
a twice-born man who had not married a wife and had not undergone the sacrament,
<s>Naravāhanadatta</s>, having a courtesan, was oppressed at night.

children.text: na dūṣaṇāyāyamudāhṛto vidhirna cābhimānena kimu pratīyate
children.translated_text: This rule has not been cited for the sake of censure, nor from arrogance. What, then, is understood?

children.text: kṛtātmanāṃ tattvadṛśāṃ ca mādṛśo jano 'bhisaṃdhiṃ ka ivāvabhotsyate ||
children.translated_text: Who could understand the intention of people like me, or of those perfected in self and seeing reality?
Now what is faulty through the absence of proposition, reason, and the rest is described
briefly and according to <s>nyāya</s>, merely for the understanding of that much meaning.
For the most part, people of poor understanding are frightened away from śāstra because it is hard to understand;
for attracting them to it, this is a gathering of a little of reasoning and <s>nyāya</s>.
People make use even of śāstra when it is mixed with the sweet flavor of poetry;
after first licking honey, they drink bitter medicine.

children.text: na sa śabdo na tadvācyaṃ na sa nyāyo na sā kalā
children.translated_text: There is no word, no meaning denoted by it, no rule of reasoning, and no art

children.text: jāyate yanna kāvyāṅgamaho bhāro mahān kaveḥ ||
children.translated_text: that is born without becoming a limb of poetry. Ah, how great is the poet's burden!
Existence and the rest are known through the two means of valid knowledge, perception and inference;
and, it is said, those two have particular and general objects respectively.
Perception, some say, is free from conceptual construction and arises from the object;
they acknowledge conceptual construction as the application of class and the like.
Such superimposition, they say, amounts only to this much, and that depends on a real object.

children.text: jātyādyapohe vṛttiḥ kva kva viśeṣaḥ kutaśca saḥ ||
children.translated_text: When class and the rest are excluded, where can its operation be, and whence could any particularity arise?

children.text: tadapoheṣu ca tathā siddhā sā buddhigocarā
children.translated_text: And when those exclusions too are excluded, it is established in that same way as something accessible to cognition.
If perception is without an object, it is false; for its operation is toward reality.
If, through the distinction between grasped object and grasper, an aspect of cognition is accepted,
then, since this is cognition alone, the particularity of it is merely a conceptual construction, because of similarity.
It is from the object alone, from form and the like, and from that alone, not from anything else.
Otherwise cognition of a pot would be designated by something different.
Some who know that subject regard inferential knowledge as arising from a threefold mark,
while others regard it as the perception of an inseparably connected object.
The subject, qualified by the property-bearer through a property resting in various loci,
is called the thesis when it is stated.
It is faulty when it contradicts its own object, the reason, established doctrine, or every accepted tradition,
when it has a contrary property, or when it is contradicted by perception.
For by that very thesis there is a production of contradiction against that object, as in:
'The ascetic is my father from childhood, whose legitimate son I am.'
'The self exists,' or 'primary matter exists' should be known as an invalidating of the reason;
because the property-bearer here is unestablished, its property too will not be established.
When the property-bearer, sound, is established, the dispute between the two disputants arises
over the difference of whether it is eternal or non-eternal.
A thesis should be known as contradicting established doctrine when it contradicts one's own doctrine,
as when <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> were to declare sound imperishable.
It contradicts every accepted tradition because it is opposed to all treatises,

children.text: yathā śucistanuḥ straiṇī tatpramāṇāni santi vā ||
children.translated_text: as in, 'A woman's body is pure,' or 'there are authoritative proofs for that.'
When a well-known property is, from childhood on, qualified by an unambiguous particular,
it is considered a famous property, as in 'sound is grasped by the ear.'
A thesis contradicted by perception is refuted by that very means of knowledge,
as in 'fire is cold,' 'color does not exist,' or 'the moon is hot.'
A reason should be known as having three characteristics: it exists in the subject, is established in what is similar,
and is excluded from what is opposed; a fallacious reason is the reverse.
That which is established as existing in both, in one's own side and the opponent's side,
is a subject with an undifferentiated definition; because of difference in result, this is twofold.
If the opponent's side is not taken up, and if its occurrence is not illustrated,
how can there be the determination of a fallacious reason that is unestablished for one of the two?
That which exists there, similar because it follows the property to be proved,
though it may be another thing, is figuratively treated as one because of commonality.
The opposite instance is dissimilar to that, since the reason is absent there and excluded from it.
Thus conformity with the two and exclusion are the valid defining marks.
An example is said to be established by the properties of what is to be proved and what proves it,
or, by the reverse, to be a semblance of that, because the reason does not occur there.
An example is that by which the accompaniment of the sign by the probandum,
and its absence when that is absent, are made known; others say that it is twofold.
A statement of deficiency and the like among objections is called deficient, and here deficiency by reason and the rest is meant.
Since the discussion is rooted in that, deficiency by the thesis is not accepted.
The <s>jāti</s>s are semblances of objections; they have equality of similarity and the like as their answers.
Their detailed expansion is manifold, but because it is extensive it is not stated here.
Another definition of reasoning, dependent on poetry, will be stated.
This much has been explained as it appears in poems that contain treatises within them.
Now, if a cause observed in the world is invariably connected and eternal,

children.text: kāraṇaṃ cen na tannityaṃ nityaṃ cet kāraṇaṃ na tat ||
children.translated_text: then if it is a cause it is not eternal, and if it is eternal it is not a cause.
In the treatises, the establishment of argument, alliance, and the like for proof
is taught in various ways according to the distinctions of definitions, applications, and faults.
By those who know them, that same matter has been brought forth differently in poetic applications.
There poetry rests on ordinary usage, while the authoritative traditions teach reality.
The sky is like a sword; sound is to be apprehended from afar;
or the same is the stability of rivers; ah, the great flame!
Just as substance is the support of form and the like and is perishable, so the thesis
which accepts a desired result is acknowledged as a proposition.
Because it rests on dharma, wealth, desire, and anger, it is fourfold.
For example, having pledged, 'I will bear this old ram for my father,'
and just so carrying it by <s>Puru</s>, that pledge would be grounded in dharma.
Having pledged, at his master's command, 'I shall myself find <s>Sītā</s>,'
by <s>Hanūmat</s>, and she was found: that pledge rests on purpose or gain.
Having made the pledge, 'Today I shall carry off this daughter of <s>Mahāsena</s>,'
by <s>Vatsa</s>, and she was abducted: that rests on passion.
For example, having pledged, 'After crushing my brother's enemy, I shall drink his blood in battle,'
<s>Bhīma</s> did exactly that, helpless under anger.
The use of a pledge should under no circumstances be made elsewhere,
nor should abandonment be made of even these four.
For example, <s>Suyodhana</s>, having pledged to fast unto death,
rose again for the sake of the kingdom; thus it contradicted dharma.
<s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, saying 'When summoned to dice I shall not turn back,'
made an agreement with <s>Śakuni</s> and gambled; that contradicted material good.
From today onward I shall live like a sage, according to my word:

children.text: pituḥ priyāya yāṃ bhīṣmaścakre sā kāmabādhinī ||
children.translated_text: the pledge that <s>Bhīṣma</s> made for his father's pleasure contradicted desire.
As <s>Rāma</s>, after defeating <s>Jāmadagnya</s> in battle, made him abandon

children.text: jāmadagnyaṃ yudhā jitvā sā jñeyā kopabādhinī ||
children.translated_text: his intention to kill all kṣatriyas, that should be known as contradicting anger.
Now there is the obtaining of an accepted condition without the acceptance of an agreement.
where, even though unstated, it is accepted from the meaning, as is said:
'What is to be known by one hostile to the senses? Who is for the rejection by enemies?

children.text: ko vā gatvaramarthibhyo na yacchati dhanaṃ laghu ||
children.translated_text: Or who, going quickly to suppliants, does not give away light wealth?'

children.text: kimatyayaṃ tu yaḥ kṣepaḥ saukaryaṃ darśayatyasau
children.translated_text: But the objection that there is a transgression shows the ease of it;
this cause, having just three marks, is approved by the very intelligent even in poems.
For positive and negative concomitance alone serve for the establishment of the meaning,
as in: 'All around the expanse of forest there is this great lake.
From the cries of the ospreys and from the fragrance of the lotuses,
even a property belonging to something else establishes that, through its connection.'
Just as from smoke scraping the clouds one infers that the place has fire,
so here too a cause is understood, though its probandum is not separated out.
There is understanding of the meaning even without positive and negative concomitance, as in:
'The night came to be bright with blazing lamps, after the sun had withdrawn.'
Here the causality of the lamps' brightness lies in the withdrawal of the sun;

children.text: tasyāpi sudhiyām iṣṭā doṣāḥ prāguditās trayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: for that too, the wise accept the three faults stated before:
those produced by ignorance, doubt, knowledge, and contrary cognition, as in:
'These <s>kāśa</s> flowers steal the heart by the fragrance of their blossoms.'
'Because they are situated near water, these should be known as <s>śarārava</s> reeds;
because it has eyes with white corners, let that be taken as a <s>cakora</s>.'
Because it is not seen in the same species, it proves that it is not a <s>cakora</s>.
An example of the stated meaning is <s>pratibimbanidarśana</s> (illustration by reflection).
'Surely let it be merely a simile, since no cause is stated.'
The statement of what is to be proved and what proves it is not desired elsewhere than in the stated case.

children.text: mukhaṃ padmamivetyatra kiṃ sādhyaṃ kiṃ ca sādhanam
children.translated_text: In the expression 'the face is like a lotus,' what is to be proved and what is the means of proof?

children.text: iti prayogasya yathā kalāv api bhavāniha
children.translated_text: Thus the usage is like this, even in art:
'You are superior because you have been instructed by elders, just as men were formerly in the <s>Kṛta</s> age.'
Where the probandum and the means of proof are suggested by the example alone,
they call that a pure example, because only that is made manifest, as in:
'You are <s>Bharata</s>; you are <s>Dilīpa</s>; you yourself are <s>Aila Purūravas</s>;
you yourself are the hero <s>Pradyumna</s>; you yourself are <s>Naravāhana</s>.'
How could his virtues be suggested by just one word?
So some good poets, afraid of prolixity, use such expressions.
One supreme word is excellent; a late and inferior composition is not.
Through reversal, that makes even fame turn into its opposite.
Unpleasant, piercing the very breaths, and ungraceful even when full of rasa,

children.text: kāvyaṃ kapitthamāmraṃ vat keṣāṃcit sadṛśaṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: poetry is, for some people, like a wood-apple and a mango, as in:
'O wide abode of fame, whose feet are fit for the heads of the best kings among your subjects,

children.text: ahighnapadmasya jalāridhāmnas tavaiva nānyasya sutasya vṛttam ||
children.translated_text: the conduct of your son alone, killer of serpents and home of lotuses and waters, is such, and of no one else.'
As one adorns speech with shining jewels, with trees bending under fruit,
and with other blossoming flowers,
'On the back of <s>Sumeru</s>, variegated with beautiful emeralds and rubies, rich in fruit and young leaves, lovely in its form,
adorned with many flowers, and attended by gods, sages, and perfected beings, he stood.'
Ornaments, groves, and garlands are adorned by these components;
for speech, an utterance of meaning and sound made oblique serves as an ornament.
Others, through a desire for expansiveness, make poetry
with contradictory words, meaningless, crowded with excessive fillers, and confused, as in:
'Its bank was rich in cardamom, takkola, nāga trees, blossoming bakula creepers, sandalwood streams, blood-red lac, camphor-cakra, aguru, realgar, and dark poetic spread;

children.text: śaṅkhavrātākulāntas timimakarakulākīrṇavīcīpratāno dadhre yasyāmbur āśiḥśaśikumudasudhākṣīraśuddhāṃ sukīrtim ||
children.translated_text: inside it was crowded with masses of conches, its extent of waves was filled with schools of whales and makaras, and its mass of waters bore his good fame, pure as moonlight, white lotuses, nectar, and milk.'

children.text: iti nigaditāstāstā vācām alaṃkṛtayo mayā bahuvidhakṛtīrdṛṣṭvānyeṣāṃ svayaṃ paritarkya ca
children.translated_text: Thus these various ornaments of speech have been stated by me, after seeing the many kinds of works of others and reasoning them out myself.

children.text: prathitavacasaḥ santo'bhijñāḥ pramāṇamihāpare gurutaradhiyām asvārādhaṃ mano'kṛtabuddhibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here other good, experienced people of renowned speech are the authority; the mind of those of weighty intellect is hard to please by people of unformed understanding.
With aphorisms as its water, with words as its whirlpools, with recitation as its nether depth,
grasping verbal roots and the <s>uṇādi</s> groups, with meditation and study as its great raft,
whose far shore is seen by the steadfast and which is envied by the unintelligent,
and which is constantly enjoyed by all the female elephants of the other sciences,
without crossing this deep and inaccessible ocean of grammar,
this person cannot adorn the self-moving jewel of language.

children.text: tasya cādhigame yatnaḥ kāryaḥ kāvyaṃ vidhitsatā
children.translated_text: Therefore one who wishes to make poetry must make effort toward mastering it.

children.text: parapratyayato yattu kriyate tena kā ratiḥ ||
children.translated_text: What delight is there in what is done on the basis of another's conviction?
Speech made of words dependent on another's judgment does not give joy to good people;
it is like a charming garland of flowers worn by someone else.
This, first of all, is the chief rule: one should proceed by one's own power.
There are others called followers of <s>Sarasvatī</s>, who repeat what has been said by others.
Others say that that by which cognition of meanings arises is a word;
therefore even smoke and light would acquire wordhood with regard to other inference.
'But a collection of phonemes beginning with a has an object denoted;
because it is taught for the cognition of meaning, it is called a word.'
How can there be a meaningful aggregate of things that are individually incapable?

children.text: varṇānāṃ kramavṛttitvān nyāyyā nāpi ca saṃhatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And because phonemes occur in sequence, a simultaneous collection is not reasonable either.
Nor is an aggregate something over and above the things aggregated.
Apart from wood, walls, and earth, what other thing is imagined as a house?

children.text: tasmāt kūṭastha ityeṣā śābdī vaḥ kalpanā vṛthā
children.translated_text: Therefore this linguistic fancy of yours that it is fixed and unchanging is useless.
Where there is either perception or inference, that exists in the highest sense.
Even with oaths one should not accept the statement of those who maintain <s>sphoṭa</s>.
What conscious person would believe that there is a flower in the sky?
So many letters of this kind, expressing meanings of this kind:
for the world's practical dealings, such a convention was made long ago.
That is said to be fixed and imperishable, and different from sound;
the dull take conventional non-realities to be ultimate realities.

children.text: vinaśvaro'stu nityo vā sambandho'rthena vā satā
children.translated_text: Let the relation with an existing meaning be perishable or eternal:

children.text: namo'stu tebhyo vidvadbhyaḥ pramāṇaṃ ye'sya niścitau ||
children.translated_text: homage to those learned men who are an authority in determining this.
Others declare that a word expresses its meaning through exclusion of what is other.
And 'exclusion of what is other' is, they say, the removal of other objects.
If this word 'cow' has fulfilled its purpose by negating what is other,

children.text: janako gavi gobuddher mṛgyatām aparo dhvaniḥ ||
children.translated_text: then let another sound be sought, one that produces the cognition of cow in a cow.
Words have knowledge of meaning as their result, and one thing does not have two results.
How, then, can one word of yours have both the cognition of exclusion and the cognition of injunction as its results?
First the cognition 'cow' would arise from hearing the word 'cow',
by which the sound 'cow' is set in motion to deny what is non-cow.
Because of difference among phonemes this is divided, and phonemes are divided according to the distinctions of their own parts.

children.text: ke śabdāḥ kiṃ ca tadvācyamityaho vartma dustaram ||
children.translated_text: What are words, and what is their denoted object? Ah, this path is hard to traverse.
And they are fourfold, according to the distinctions of substance, action, genus, and quality.
Others also admit arbitrary words, such as <s>Ḍittha</s> and the like.
For words that have many languages as their sphere and operate over endless meanings,
by whom, and how, can their exact extent be especially determined?

children.text: vakravācāṃ kavīnāṃ ye prayogaṃ prati sādhavaḥ
children.translated_text: For poets whose speech is indirect, those words that are proper with respect to usage,
and those that are not fit to be used: their discrimination is now stated.
One should not use an unattested word that causes confusion in the mind.
For even when meanings are equal, who would say 'hanti' for a word expressing motion?

children.text: śrotrādiṃ na tu durbodhaṃ na duṣṭādimapeśalam
children.translated_text: Nor should one use such words as śrotrādi when they are hard to understand, nor ungraceful words such as duṣṭādi,
nor rustic words such as piṇḍīśūra, nor meaningless words such as ḍittha.
Nor should one use a word whose different meaning is not understood, because roots may have many meanings;
for example, dhyāti, when its compound form is dragged in to indicate only a slight sense.
Nor should one speak a word merely because it has been used by cultivated people, nor because it is established in another technical system,
nor, on the general ground that it is like Vedic language, should one use a Vedic form.
One should utter a meaningful word that has come down in order and is pleasant to the ear.
For beauty of expression surpasses any other ornament.
A form that is established, or that is justified by an accepted supplementary rule,

children.text: tam ādriyeta prāyeṇa na tu yogavibhāgajam ||
children.translated_text: one should generally respect; but not one produced merely by dividing a rule by etymological analysis.
This moon-faced maiden is charming by nature itself;
on her, an ornament of gold greatly increases her beauty.
One should use the strengthened form, as with the root mṛj even in a change of form:
'Those falling tear-drops wipe away the redness of your lower lip.'

children.text: sarūpaśeṣaṃ tu pumān striyā yatra ca śiṣyate
children.translated_text: Where the masculine remains as the residue of like forms together with the feminine,
as one says <s>Varuṇau</s> and <s>Indrau</s>, <s>Bhavau</s> and <s>Śarvau</s>, <s>Mṛḍau</s>, and so on.
Just as in paṭayati and similar forms, the causative suffix <s>ṇic</s> follows a nominal stem;
and by the accepted rule that it is treated like ṇāv iṣṭhavat, so too one may use kraśayati.
One should not use an avyayībhāva compound that ends in -a, nor one that is not equivalent to a fifth-case relation.
In the alternatives of the third and seventh cases, one should not introduce a case where elision is absent.
In tiṣṭhadgu and the like, the forms are to be stated when they refer to day-and-night activity,

children.text: yathā vidvānadhīte'sau tiṣṭhadgu ca vahadgu ca ||
children.translated_text: as in: 'That learned man studies both as one who keeps cows standing and as one who drives cows along.'
On the mere basis of cultivated usage, or on the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa,
one should never cite a compound with tṛc and a genitive compounded with it.
On the mere basis of an indication in a sūtra, as vṛtrahantā is stated,

children.text: akena ca na kurvīta vṛttiṃ tadgamako yathā ||
children.translated_text: one should not form a compound with aka, as in tadgamaka.

children.text: pañcarājīti ca yathā prayuñjīta dviguḥ striyām
children.translated_text: And just as one should use the dvigu compound in the feminine, as in pañcarājī,
so one may use a neuter tatpuruṣa compound, as in puruhūtasabha.
And after all words beginning with bhṛśa one should state the form with the consonant elided, as in:
'She is very dear-minded toward you; why, rogue, are you proud-minded?'

children.text: tṛtīyaikavacaḥ ṣaṣṭyām āmantaṃ ca vadet kvipi
children.translated_text: One should also use the third singular form with the sixth-case sense, and a form ending in ām when kviP is used,
as stated, in balabhidā, like the beautiful flashes of lightning.
Even if a statement is about what does not exist, one should employ it just so,
as people say, 'by the light of the waters' and 'by the water of fame.'
They say that a form ending in kvasu is acceptable in both masculine and feminine and is not Vedic-only,

children.text: upeyuṣāmapi divaṃ yathā na vyeti cārutā ||
children.translated_text: as in: 'The beauty does not depart even of those who have gone to heaven.'
The young woman, bearing breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant and like balls,
weary from the exertion of love-play, stole the hearts of men.

children.text: śabalādibhyo nitarāṃ bhāti ṇij vihito yathā
children.translated_text: From śabala and the like, the causative suffix <s>ṇic</s>, when prescribed, shines especially, as in:
'Look, fair-hipped one, those cranes make the clouds variegated.'
Like a kaṅga bird, the winter shower's tiny drops, similar to you,
fan the fair-hipped woman whose eyes are languid from the fatigue of love-play.
Thus the use of the causative suffix <s>ṇic</s> is everywhere a supreme ornament.
And the suffix <s>ṇini</s>, applicable in all three genders, concerns habitual disposition.

children.text: tasyā hārī stanābhogo vadanaṃ hāri sundaram
children.translated_text: Her expanse of breasts is captivating; her beautiful face is captivating;
her body is utterly captivating. How much does it not steal the mind?
In cases of habitual disposition and the like, all suffixes beginning with tṛn are accepted.
There, in particular, yut, kura, jvara, and jiṣṇu are specially approved.
One should also use a form ending in ktin, as in saṃgati and saṃhati.

children.text: śakārau jāgur iṣṭau ca jāgaryā jāgarā yathā ||
children.translated_text: The syllables śa and ka are also approved in jāgari, as in jāgaryā and jāgarā.

children.text: upāsaneti ca yucaṃ nityam āseḥ prayojayet
children.translated_text: And for the root ās, one should always employ yuc, as in upāsanā.

children.text: lyuṭaṃ ca kartṛviṣayaṃ devano ramaṇo yathā ||
children.translated_text: And lyuṭ should be used when the agent is meant, as in devana and ramaṇa.
Even after stems ending in -aṇ and the like, the suffix ṅīb is desired, as in lakṣmī and pauraṃdarī.
And after mahārajan, likewise, ṭhak is prescribed with lākṣā and rocanā.
And ḍmatup is desired with words such as kumuda; thus this earth is called kumudvatī.

children.text: ṭhak cāpi tena jayatītyākṣikaḥ śāstriko yathā ||
children.translated_text: And ṭhak also occurs in such expressions as 'he wins by that,' as in ākṣika and śāstrika.
In the section on what is beneficial, they use ṇa also after the word sarva.

children.text: tataśchamiṣṭhyā ca yathā sārvaḥ sarvīya ityapi ||
children.translated_text: From that, with chamiṣṭhyā and the like, one may get forms such as sārva and also sarvīya.

children.text: vaded imanijantaṃ ca paṭimā laghimā yathā
children.translated_text: One should also state forms ending in imanic, as in paṭimā and laghimā.
In a special sense, īyasun is desired, as in jyāyān and also kanīyasī.
Dvayasa, dadhna, and ca are used with reference to measure,
as in a river knee-deep, and a lake reaching the two hips of a woman.
The matup section includes words such as jyotsnā, tamisrā, and śṛṅgin.
And inac is used after phala and barha, as in phalin and barhin.

children.text: iniḥ prayuktaḥ prāyeṇa tathā ṭhaṃśca manīṣibhiḥ
children.translated_text: The suffix ini is generally used, and so too ṭha, by learned men.
There too it is especially approved after mekhalā, mālā, and māyā.
When ad is substituted for jhi after reduplicated stems, forms such as dadhati also occur.
Forms such as roditi and svapiti take the sārvadhātuka ending with iṭ.

children.text: abhyasteṣu prayoktavyam adantaṃ ca videḥ śatuḥ
children.translated_text: Among reduplicated forms it should be used; and the participial śatṛ of vid is without final a.
This man shines, holding ornaments and wearing a garland.
One should call him a yogin.
For example: 'This dark forest shines, lotus-eyed lady.'
An excess of the vowel au should not occur in one place, as in gataḥ, yātaḥ, and hataḥ.
One should say the bha-form in the case of sāvarṇya and vatsa, not elsewhere, according to the traditional rule.

children.text: sālāturīyamatam etadanukrameṇa ko vakṣyatīti virato'hamato vicārāt
children.translated_text: This is the doctrine of the master from Sālātura; who could set it forth in proper sequence? Therefore I have ceased from that inquiry.

children.text: śabdārṇavasya yadi kaścidupaiti pāraṃ bhīmāmbhasaśca jaladheriti vismayo'sau ||
children.translated_text: If anyone reaches the far shore of the ocean of words, and of the sea with its terrible waters, that is a wonder indeed.

children.text: vidyānāṃ satatamapāśrayo'parāsāṃ tāsūktānna ca viruṇaddhi kāṃścidarthān
children.translated_text: It is always the support of the other sciences, and from what is stated in them it does not obstruct any meanings.

children.text: śraddheyaṃ jagati mataṃ hi pāṇinīyaṃ mādhyasthyād bhavati na kasyacitpramāṇam ||
children.translated_text: For the Pāṇinian doctrine is worthy of trust in the world; because of its impartiality, it is not an authority belonging to anyone in particular.

children.text: avalokya matāni satkavīnām avagamya svadhiyā ca kāvyalakṣma
children.translated_text: Having examined the opinions of good poets and having understood the marks of poetry through his own intelligence,
this work has been composed by <s>Bhāmaha</s>, son of <s>Rakrilagomin</s>, for the understanding of good people.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the venerable <s>Bhāmahālaṃkāra</s>.
With sixty verses the body of poetry has been determined, and with one hundred and sixty, its ornamentation.
With fifty verses there is the examination of faults, and with seventy, the determination of logic.
With sixty verses there is the purity of language; thus this fivefold subject matter
has been stated for you in order by <s>Bhāmaha</s> in six chapters.
